title: Leaderboard
story: The gaming tournament just ended and you have the scores — Alice: 850, Bob: 920, Carol: 780, Dave: 950. The crowd is chanting for the top three. You need to sort these players by score and announce the winners!
why: Maps store key-value pairs for fast lookups, and manual sorting teaches you to extract ordered information from unordered data — a fundamental skill in data processing.
analogy: A Map is like a phone book — you flip to a name (key) and read their number (value). The book doesn't sort by number, but you can scan through all entries to find the top three numbers.
try_it: Add three more players with higher scores (e.g., 1000, 1100, 1200). Does the top 3 update? Then modify the code to show top 5 instead of top 3. What happens if two players have the same score? Write a tie-breaker that sorts alphabetically when scores are equal.
tips: Maps are unordered — use a separate Vec to iterate keys in a known order
`.get(&key)` returns `Option[V]` — always match to handle the `None` case safely
The `&` in `.get(&key)` creates a borrow — Map looks up by reference, not by value
common_mistakes: Calling `scores.get(key)` without `&` — Map.get expects a borrowed key: `scores.get(&key)`
Assuming Map has an order — Map entries are NOT sorted; you must sort manually
Forgetting to check both Map and Vec for the same data — if you add to Map but not Vec, iteration misses entries
